#10265. What Is the Best UI design Tool? 8 Tools Compared by the Job They Do (2026)

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

The ideal UI testing tool is the one that discovers what your users discover first: broken layouts, usability issues that no longer work, and new accessibility issues in all the browsers your users use before a change goes into the repository. In 2026, most frontend teams don't rely on a single tool to do all of that. The best setups involve two layers: a test runner layer that launches the browser and monitors behavior, and a UI testing and review platform that visually checks the outcome and routes changes to the right stakeholders for sign-off.

Even with the right stack, it still relies on what your team needs to catch. Different teams will focus on different points: a QA team trying to automate checkout flows, a design system team defending shared components, and a single developer working on a tight budget will all be somewhere different. This guide is categorized by the job these UI testing tools do, then connects them.

Most "best UI testing tool" lists rank test runners and visual testing platforms against each other as if they were interchangeable. They aren't. UI testing covers four distinct jobs:

Functional testing: Does the UI respond correctly when a user clicks, types, or hovers?

Visual testing: Does the UI still look right across layout, color, typography, and spacing?

Accessibility testing: Can people using keyboards and screen readers use it, and did this change introduce new violations?

Cross-browser and device coverage: Does it work in Safari on mobile, not just Chrome on a developer's laptop?

There are also other levels of UI tests. Unit tests test the logic but don't interact with the UI. End-to-end (E2E) tests represent the full user journey in a browser but are difficult to set up, hard to troubleshoot when the bug is a visual detail, and can't practically test every state. Between the extremes of unit tests and E2E tests, component tests simulate each component's behavior in a real browser using fixed inputs, offering speed closer to unit tests and user-level coverage closer to E2E. Many teams maintain a thin layer of E2E tests for critical journeys, and they have component tests for the dozens of states a component may be in.

These tools are organized by job so you can stack them rather than choose one winner

These platforms sit on top of your test runner. They capture rendered UI, compare it to approved baselines, and give your team a place to review what changed.

Chromatic is a UI testing and review platform made by the Storybook team. It catches visual, interaction, and accessibility bugs in components and pages before they merge, and it gives developers, designers, and product managers one place to review UI changes and sign off. Chromatic's team is the core maintainer of Storybook, which has about 90,000 GitHub stars and 17 million weekly npm downloads, and a Vitest core maintainer on the team built Chromatic's Vitest integration. Chromatic is used by 45 Fortune 100 companies, including GitHub, Shopify, Microsoft, Adobe, the BBC, and monday.com.

Pricing: Free plan with 5,000 snapshots per month (Chrome only), unlimited projects and users. Starter is $179/month for 35,000 snapshots and adds Safari, Firefox, and Edge. Pro is $399/month for 85,000 snapshots. Enterprise is custom, with SSO, SCIM, SLA support, and data retention. TurboSnap snapshots count as 0.2 of a regular snapshot.

Trade-offs: Chromatic is strongest when your UI is built from components. Teams with no component tests can start from Playwright or Cypress E2E tests, but they'll get the most value once components are covered too. Snapshot usage also grows with each browser and viewport you add, so plan coverage before you scale it.

Best for: Design system teams, product teams that want designers and PMs to approve UI changes, React Native teams, and Vitest-first teams that want visual testing without baselines stored in the repo.

Percy is BrowserStack's visual testing platform. It captures screenshots from your existing tests, renders them across browsers and responsive widths, and highlights pixel differences for review.

Strengths: Framework-agnostic SDKs for Playwright, Cypress, Selenium, and Storybook. App Percy covers native mobile apps. The free plan includes 5,000 screenshots per month with unlimited users and projects.

Trade-offs: Percy is page-oriented, and each page rendered in each browser at each width counts as a separate screenshot, so usage climbs quickly with cross-browser coverage. Percy compares feature branches against a base branch, which teams with complex branching should test early. Reviewers see rendered screenshots rather than an inspectable copy of the code under test, so debugging a diff usually means reproducing it locally.

Pricing: Free tier, then paid plans with fixed screenshot allowances and overage.

Best for: Teams already paying for BrowserStack that want visual checks on page-level E2E tests.

Applitools Eyes uses Visual AI to compare screenshots the way a person would, with match levels that can ignore content changes and focus on layout. Its Ultrafast Grid re-renders captured page states across many browser, viewport, and device combinations.

Strengths: Mature AI matching, broad browser and device coverage, Figma and Storybook testing, accessibility testing, and an MCP server. Higher tiers add AI-driven functional testing and plain-English test authoring.

Trade-offs: Applitools is priced and packaged for enterprises. There's a free trial but no free plan, and the Starter plan is $667/month billed annually for 100,000 component checkpoints or 1,000 page checkpoints. Professional and Enterprise are custom-priced.

Best for: Large QA organizations with big cross-browser matrices and budget for a dedicated visual AI platform.

BackstopJS is a free, open-source visual regression testing tool released under the MIT license. You list the URLs, viewports, and CSS selectors to capture in a config file, and BackstopJS renders them in a headless browser through Playwright or Puppeteer, then compares the results against approved reference screenshots. The core workflow runs on three commands: backstop init, backstop test, and backstop approve.

Strengths: Completely free, with no screenshot limits. A built-in browser report shows reference and test images side by side with a visual diff inspector, and changes can be approved from there. Optional Docker rendering keeps screenshots consistent between laptops and CI; Playwright adds Firefox and WebKit, and click, hover, and keypress selectors capture interactive states. JUnit reports plug into existing CI pipelines.

Trade-offs: BackstopJS is self-hosted, so there's no cloud dashboard, shared team review, or pull request status checks out of the box. Reference screenshots are usually committed to your repository, and every page or component state you want to test needs its own URL and scenario in the config. Someone on the team also has to own the setup, CI integration, and maintenance.

Best for: Developers and small teams with no budget who are comfortable running and maintaining their own visual regression setup.

Test runners click, type, and assert. They're free and open source, and every platform above builds on them. On their own, they offer limited visual testing: built-in screenshot assertions store baselines in your repository, rendering can drift between laptops and CI, and designers have no review interface.

Playwright is Microsoft's open-source browser automation framework. It runs tests across Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit, with auto-waiting, trace viewer debugging and code generation, and supports JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java, and .NET.

Visual testing: Playwright's toHaveScreenshot assertion compares screenshots against baselines stored in Git. It works, but baselines must be regenerated per operating system, and accepting a change means rerunning with an update flag.

Best for: Teams automating critical user journeys such as sign-up, checkout and login. Pair it with a platform like Chromatic for visual review across real browsers.

Cypress is an open-source testing tool that runs inside the browser, with time-travel debugging that shows the app at each step of a test. It supports both E2E and component testing.

Visual testing: Cypress has no built-in visual comparison and relies on plugins or a platform such as Chromatic, Percy or Applitools. Cypress Cloud, its paid service, adds recording, parallelization, flake detection and add-ons for accessibility and UI coverage.

Best for: Frontend developers who want fast feedback and an interactive test runner while they build.

Storybook is the open source workshop for building UI components in isolation. Each story captures one component state, and those stories double as test cases.

Testing features: Interaction tests with play functions and Testing Library, accessibility checks with the a11y addon, and a Vitest integration that runs stories as component tests.

Visual testing: Storybook doesn't diff screenshots on its own. Chromatic, built by the same team, is its visual testing and review layer.

Best for: Design system and component library teams, and any team practicing component-driven development.

Vitest Browser Mode runs component tests in a real browser instead of a simulated DOM, using Playwright or WebdriverIO under the hood.

Visual testing: Vitest's toMatchScreenshot assertion stores screenshots in the repository. For large projects, this can bloat the repo and baselines drift between machines. Chromatic can take Vitest Browser Mode tests with no code changes and run them in a stable cloud environment instead.

Best for: Teams already writing Vitest tests who want them to check how the UI looks without adopting a new framework.

Start from the problem your team is trying to fix:

"Shared component changes keep breaking other teams' screens." Test at the component level with Storybook or Vitest Browser Mode and Chromatic, so the change shows up on the pull request that caused it.

"Our Playwright tests pass, but the layout still breaks in Safari." Functional assertions don't check appearance. Add a visual testing platform that renders in Safari, such as Chromatic, Percy or Applitools.

"We turned off screenshot tests because of false alarms." Look for deterministic component states and flake controls such as Chromatic's SteadySnap, or AI matching such as Applitools.

"Designers find UI bugs after release." Choose a platform with a review and approval workflow, and make sign-off a required pull request check.

"AI coding agents keep inventing components." Give agents access to your real component library, for example through Chromatic's hosted MCP, and run every agent-built change through the same UI tests as human code.

"We have no budget." Use Playwright or Vitest screenshot assertions, self-host BackstopJS, or start on the free tiers of Chromatic or Percy.

A practical, well-covered setup for a React web app looks like this:

Unit tests in Vitest for logic and utilities.

Storybook stories or Vitest Browser Mode tests for every meaningful component state, with interaction tests on key components.

Chromatic running visual, interaction and accessibility tests on those components in Chrome, Firefox, Safari and Edge on every pull request, with designers assigned as reviewers.

A thin layer of Playwright E2E tests for sign-up, checkout and other critical journeys, also captured in Chromatic so page-level visual changes go through the same review.

This keeps most UI coverage in fast, deterministic component tests, while E2E tests confirm the journeys that matter most still work end to end.

Playwright is the best free tool for E2E UI testing, and Storybook is the best free tool for testing component states. For visual testing, For visual testing, Chromatic and Percy both offer free tiers of around 5,000 snapshots or screenshots per month, and BackstopJS is free to self-host.

UI testing is the broad practice of checking that an interface works for users, including functional, visual and accessibility checks. Visual testing is one part of it: comparing rendered UI against approved baselines to catch unintended changes in layout, color, typography and spacing.

No. Chromatic was built by the Storybook team, but it also runs visual tests from Vitest Browser Mode, Playwright and Cypress tests, and from React Native Storybook on iOS and Android simulators.

Playwright's toHaveScreenshot covers basic visual checks, but baselines live in your repo, rendering can differ between machines, and there's no review interface for designers. Teams with several reviewers or many browsers usually add a platform on top.

Most teams use both. Component tests cover individual UI states quickly and reliably, while a smaller set of E2E tests confirms that critical user journeys work across the whole app.

#10262. Why your HSA needs a succession plan

Health savings accounts are usually discussed in the context of their trifecta of tax benefits: pretax money going in, tax-free compounding while the funds are inside the account, and tax-free withdrawals for qualified healthcare expenditures.

But HSAs have their limits. The HSA’s tax benefits effectively cease upon the account owner’s death, or the death of his or her spouse if that person is the beneficiary.

That makes it crucial to have a succession plan for your HSA: a plan to encourage tax-free spending during your lifetime (and your spouse’s, if you have one), as well as naming the correct beneficiary for the account to maximize the tax benefits.

HSAs give during your lifetime . . .

Whereas tax-sheltered retirement account owners will pay taxes on the dollars they put into a retirement account (Roth) or on their withdrawals (traditional tax-deferred), HSAs are a unicorn account type—the funds are tax-free every step of the way, provided you spend the money on qualified healthcare expenses.

Those tax benefits are magnified for people who pay their healthcare expenses out of pocket, invest in long-term investment assets, and are in higher tax brackets.

Given those prodigious tax benefits, an HSA investor would have a bigger balance than a person investing in an IRA, 401(k), or taxable brokerage account, assuming the same contribution amounts, rates of return, tax rates, and holding periods. That’s because investors in those other account types pay taxes along the way: at time of contribution (Roth), during accumulation (taxable), and/or at time of withdrawal (taxable, traditional tax-deferred).

. . . And take after death

If your spouse is the designated beneficiary of your HSA, the HSA becomes theirs after your death, and the tax benefits continue. They can continue to take tax-free withdrawals for qualified healthcare expenses.

But if a person other than your spouse inherits the HSA, the account becomes less attractive than the other key account types mentioned before. An HSA inherited by a nonspouse beneficiary effectively ceases to be an HSA upon the account owner’s death, and all of its tax benefits go away at that time. Moreover, the nonspouse beneficiary will need to include the inherited HSA amount in their income and pay taxes on it.

The tax treatment of an HSA inherited by a nonspouse beneficiary is a bit worse than the tax treatment of other major account types that nonspouse beneficiaries might inherit. Heirs enjoy tax-free withdrawals on inherited Roth accounts. Traditional IRA beneficiaries owe taxes, but they at least enjoy some flexibility on the timing of their withdrawals and tax bills. Heirs inheriting taxable accounts have it even better, in that their cost basis becomes whatever the account holdings’ values were on the date of your death.

You need a plan for handling your HSA

That meh tax treatment on HSAs inherited by nonspouse beneficiaries highlights the value of having a plan to maximize your HSA’s long-term tax benefits.

Step 1: Get a system for spending from it

Spending from the HSA during your and your spouse’s lifetimes is key, so every HSA owner needs a spending plan. That’s true whether you’re paying healthcare expenses as you incur them or investing the funds for retirement.

If you’ve been paying your healthcare costs out of pocket in an effort to allow your account to grow, you can later use the HSA for non-healthcare expenses, provided you have receipts to substantiate those previous out-of-pocket healthcare costs. Ideally, you’d scan and document those expenditures as you incur them. If you’re a married person who’s overseeing your household’s HSA, make sure your spouse understands the withdrawal rules, where to find receipts, and how to submit them to the HSA provider.

Step 2: Assign the correct beneficiaries

Next, give care to naming beneficiaries. If you’re married, your spouse is a sensible beneficiary for the HSA; as noted earlier, they will be able to take over ownership of the account after your death and keep its full tax benefits during their lifetime.

Nonspouse beneficiaries won’t receive the same favorable tax treatment. However, if you think a nonspouse beneficiary still will benefit from the money, that’s probably a good enough reason to leave them the HSA. But other accounts should take precedence.

A charity can also make an excellent HSA beneficiary, as the charity won’t need to pay taxes on that amount. That strategy can be particularly appropriate for single people who are charitably inclined, or for surviving spouses. If you’re married, consider making your spouse the primary beneficiary and a charity the secondary.

Step 3: Make sure your beneficiaries understand the rules about HSAs

If your spouse will inherit your HSA, be sure to underscore the value of liquidating the account during his or her lifetime.

While it’s generally not advisable for a nonspouse beneficiary to inherit an HSA, if that’s your plan, it’s important to let your loved ones know that they can reduce the taxable amount in the HSA by paying any of your unpaid medical bills from the HSA. They just need to pay those bills out of your HSA within a year of your death.

This article was provided to The Associated Press by Morningstar. For more retirement content, go to morningstar.com/retirement.

#10258. Why your boss can basically fire you for anything—and why it’s not like that outside the U.S.

We’ve all seen the scene play out in media: A character stands up at work, dramatically declares they quit, and walks out of the office for the last time. While many people will surely empathize with that desire, the reason why a sudden resignation is possible in the U.S. isn’t as great as such a display makes it out to be. 

Mostly because it goes both ways: an employer can axe you at the drop of a hat, in theory—even without a warning, PIP, or other chance to improve.

The U.S. has something called at-will employment, which means that you can leave—or lose—your job without giving any notice.

A job that’s at-will “can end at any moment, for good reason, bad reason, or no reason at all, and with no procedural mandates,” says Gali Racabi, an assistant professor at Cornell’s School of Industrial and Labor Relations and an associated faculty member of Cornell Law School. 

Currently, at-will employment is the law of the land in Washington, D.C., and every U.S. state except Montana. 

“This makes work in the US really easy to sever,” Racabi says.

He adds: “The at-will rule is a travesty, and a mark of moral flaw in our economic order. We need to do away with it ASAP.” 

Critiques of at-will employment

Despite being the default in America—a country whose culture is associated with entrepreneurialism, independence and one that favors employers without much safety-net protection for workers—at-will employment causes a number of concerns. 

Most prominent, perhaps, is a person suddenly losing their income and the many repercussions that can come with that. The practice is also especially risky in the U.S., where individuals often rely on their job for necessary benefits like healthcare—something many other nations provide outside of employment, Racabi says. Say, for instance, a person has an operation scheduled for next week and gets laid off today. Suddenly, they don’t have coverage for a necessary procedure. 

That’s a more extreme example. But even losing health insurance without a big medical issue coming up, and no time to find an alternative, can have devastating repercussions around the cost of medicine, seeing a doctor, or having security in an emergency. 

At-will employment can also complicate the process of proving retaliation or discrimination as the reason for a layoff. 

“Having the at-will rule also makes it really difficult to enforce other work-related laws, like anti-discrimination law,” says Racabi. “If an employer can simply terminate someone without notice, reason, or hearing, it makes proving discriminatory intent extremely hard.” The employer doesn’t have to prove any other justification for the firing.

In a 2022 survey from the National Employment Law Project, 69% of U.S. workers who had experienced a layoff or firing reported that they were either given no or an unfair reason. On top of that, 72% of these participants reported being terminated without a chance to improve or any warning. Overall, 66% of workers surveyed said they support the enactment of just-cause policies. 

Of course, not everyone thinks at-will employment should be thrown out. Carson Young, an associate professor at West Virginia University’s John Chambers College of Business and Economics, argues that at-will employment is “complicated.” It can allow workers to earn higher salaries and have more flexibility than with a just cause system, since the setup potentially lowers employer costs around hiring extra people, with less incentive to keep anyone onboard. 

Young also believes that at-will employment grants workers more freedom to leave a job as they please. He also argues that it could also make employers more likely to hire new employees, as they don’t have to make as big of a commitment to the employee if it ends up not being a good fit, a project ends, or the thing they were hired for doesn’t work out. 

“Employers in [countries] with more job protections are thus more reluctant to hire, because they face greater costs if the hire doesn’t work out,” Young says. 

How the U.S. compares to other countries

The U.S. is fairly unique in having at-will employment, with many other developed countries requiring just cause and notice to terminate an employee. In turn, the individual is often also required to provide notice when leaving a position.

“U.S. courts tend to favor freedom of contract and employer-employee flexibility over job security,” says Young. But “employment law in most other countries places a greater emphasis on job security over freedom of contract and flexibility.”

In the U.K., arguably the country most directly compared to the U.S., an employer can only let you go for “a valid reason that they can justify” and if they’ve “acted reasonably in the circumstance.” An employer will also typically have to give notice of a layoff between one to 12 weeks prior to termination, depending on the length of employment. An employee must give at least a week’s notice, but it can be longer depending on their contract. 

Yet, the U.K. also has zero-hour contracts—which mean an employer doesn’t have to guarantee any work and the individual, in turn, doesn’t have to accept any. These casual contracts are common in positions such as retail or hospitality. 

Critics of the U.K.’s zero-hour contracts point to issues similar to that of at-will employment: Workers on zero-hour contracts “will find it difficult to plan their ordinary lives and pay their bills because they are guaranteed no shifts and will find they have no regular or fixed income stream,” says David Cabrelli, a professor of labor law at the University of Edinburgh’s Law School. 

“Seen from the perspective of job and earnings security, both employment-at-will and zero-hours contracts put workers in a very vulnerable and precarious position.”

Could the U.S. get rid of at-will employment?

The U.K.’s Employment Rights Act 2025 has set new regulations for zero-hour contracts, including a right to guaranteed hours and pay for last-minute shift cancellations. The changes have not yet rolled out, with some employers and unions criticizing the new measures, the Guardian reports. 

Generally, the U.S. is not typically seen as a country that strongly values workers’ rights, instead valuing the good of the employer or business. But could the U.S. also pursue changes? 

Some caveats already exist in circumstances such as whistle-blowing or alleging sexual harassment. “However, these exceptions are issue-specific and the legal position could be improved for workers by the introduction of a just cause dismissal regime,” says Cabrelli. 

So, then, could just cause ever become the law of the land in the U.S.—a place where workers’ rights are rarely prioritized? 

“At-will is law, and we can change laws,” says Racabi. “We can enact statutory just-cause or procedural mandate laws at the federal, state, and local levels. We can do those without significant legal pushback. 

Racabi continues: “We can also support unionization; that one of its byproducts is increased workers’ protection via collective bargaining agreements.” 

At-will employment might be the norm in the U.S., but that doesn’t mean it’s the best option. Or that it has to be around forever.

With that 1,200 GPD capacity, it can keep up with heavier day-to-day use as well as busier holiday hosting without slowing things down.

The X12 is certified to NSF/ANSI 42, 58, and 372 standards, and it has picked up some notable recognition too, including being named “Best Smart Reverse Osmosis Water System” by Forbes Vetted in 2026 and appearing in The New York Times Wirecutter’s roundup of the best reverse osmosis systems.

The X12 is easily one of the standout options in Waterdrop Filter’s Black Friday lineup, and it’s worth considering if you’re looking for a long-term under sink reverse osmosis upgrade and want strong flow, advanced filtration, and plenty of everyday convenience.

You don’t necessarily need a huge kitchen or a large family to make the jump to a proper RO setup, and that’s where the latest Waterdrop G6A6 Reverse Osmosis System comes in. This compact model is down to $189.99 shipped from its $300 usual price for Black Friday, and you use promo code 9TO5GBF26 to score an extra 5% off, making it one of the more affordable options in Waterdrop Filter’s under-sink lineup this year. The biggest advantage of the G6A6 system is its compact design, which Waterdrop says can save up to 81.8% of under-sink space. That makes it a particularly good fit for apartments, smaller kitchens, or any setup where you don’t want a bulky filtration system taking up most of the cabinet.

Despite the smaller footprint, though, this model can delivers up to 600 gallons per day, which should be more than enough for the everyday drinking, cooking, and beverage needs of a smaller household. Its eight-stage filtration system is also paired with alkaline remineralization to add minerals such as calcium and magnesium back for a better-tasting water.

It’s safe to say the Waterdrop G6A6 is probably the more sensible pick over stepping up to something as powerful as the X12 if you have a smaller family of three or four, or you’re simply working with limited kitchen space.

If you’d rather skip an under-sink installation altogether, the Waterdrop M6HG Mineral Instant Hot Reverse Osmosis System is another solid option in the sale. This newer 2026 countertop model is down to $299 shipped from its usual $429 price right now, and the promo code 9TO5GBF26 gets you an extra 5% off for additional savings. This particular model gives you filtered water plus instant heating in one compact setup without any plumbing required.

#10254. Utah asks to drop criminal charges against Kalshi and its founders

Utah asked a court to dismiss the criminal charges it filed last month against prediction market operator Kalshi and two of its executives, citing Kalshi’s decision to halt trading in the state that had accused it of running an illegal gambling enterprise.

The one-sentence motion filed Tuesday in a Salt Lake City-based court by state Attorney General Derek Brown referenced a “change in circumstance.” Brown’s office noted that it could refile the case if Kalshi resumes offering trades on its platform there.

“Kalshi has pulled out of Utah, and if it returns, so will the charges,” Brown said in a statement.

Utah has been on the front lines of a battle between states and the federal government over who regulates the markets. Litigation has spread across more than 20 states, creating a fragmented legal landscape that analysts say will likely be settled by the U.S. Supreme Court.

The felony charges filed by Utah include 13 counts of violating the state’s prohibition on gambling and another charge involving profiting off illegal activity.

The state’s charging documents name Kalshi and its cofounders, chief executive officer Tarek Mansour and chief operating officer Luana Lopes Lara. They are due in court in Salt Lake City on December 4, unless a judge agrees to dismiss the case.

Utah law prohibits gambling, and Utah considers prediction markets gambling, Brown’s office said. Many other states contend that the platforms’ sports trading activities are flouting their laws that regulate sports betting and casino gambling.

Utah’s felony charges represented a new tactic in how states are trying to assert regulatory authority over the fast-expanding activity. Brown’s office also has asked a court to make Kalshi give up the profits it made in Utah.

Kalshi, the nation’s largest prediction market operator, said Monday it had halted trading in Utah after it became clear that a federal judge hearing a case brought by the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) wouldn’t immediately stop Utah’s attempts to shut it down there.

A Kalshi spokeswoman called it an “unfortunate outcome for the more than 177,000 Utahns who use Kalshi” but said the company will continue to fight in court for the right to operate in Utah.

Kalshi, like the CFTC, argues that prediction markets offer “event contracts” that should be considered swaps under a federal law that grants exclusive regulation to the federal agency. Utah and at least 44 other states have opposed that view.

Kalshi sued Utah in February, asking a federal judge to prevent the state from enforcing its gambling restrictions on the platform. A federal judge rejected the request, and an appeal is pending.

Trading activity on Kalshi is halted in Nevada and partially in Michigan and Washington, according to Kalshi.

—By Marc Levy, Associated Press

#10252. Samsung fans continue to hate on Galaxy S27 Ultra redesign

An alleged new video shows Galaxy S27 dummy units that look like the latest leaks, and Samsung fans aren’t having it.

At this point, it’s anyone’s best guess as to what the Galaxy S27 series looks like, but it’s seeming surer and surer that Samsung will be giving the series a big redesign this coming year. Chris Franklin, a writer at SammyGuru, posted an unboxing video of the Galaxy S27 on X, citing that there’s a possibility the unboxing is AI-created — there are some eyebrow-raising reflections here, but it’s hard to tell for certain. The design looks similar to the “confirmed” renders that leaked a few days ago, although there are some subtle differences.

I don't think much about the design of phones, they're essentially all the same, especially when considering you're looking at the front 90% of the time, but I've always found the Galaxy's vertical camera layout to be the least attractive of any of the major phones. I think this looks much better.

Unsurprisingly, another leak from earlier in the month has a similar look but, again, with subtle differences. So far, all the major leaks in the past few months are pointing to Samsung outfitting the Galaxy S27 series with a raised camera island that looks extremely similar to Apple’s design on the iPhone 17 Pro and 18 Pro series.

Samsung isn’t alone here. The Xiaomi 18 series and Honor Magic 9 Pro series both have eerily similar designs, and many other 2026 and 2027 phones have followed suit. The most obvious problem with Samsung’s potential design (and, by extension, Apple’s) is the raised camera lenses, which protrude above the raised camera island. Xiaomi’s island is flat, following Google’s idea that a camera bar should protect the lenses and also keep the phone from wobbling or feeling off-balance.

Drama has already taken off on X (formerly Twitter), where Noah Cat reposted the video, and it seems Samsung fans aren’t happy. Samsung has needed to change up the vertical camera bar for years, as it has regularly gotten in the way of Qi2 and MagSafe magnetic accessories. This new design might help that, but it seems fans wanted Samsung to return to the Galaxy S10 horizontal camera bar days, not this new iPhone-esque raised island.

#10251. Elon Musk once again promises Tesla’s new autonomous driving is better than humans

Elon Musk has a new promise: Version 15 of Full Self-Driving drives better than a real driver. “Completely new architecture that deserves being called ‘super’ intelligence, as it drives better than human intelligence,” he wrote on X after Tesla started sending the update to a first batch of owners.

That’s great news.

It was great news back in November 2023, too, when he wrote: “Over time, Version 12 (end-to-end neural nets) will far exceed human safety even when unsupervised.” Also in August 2025, when he said: “v14 will be better than human for sure, but I don’t know if it will be 10X. Maybe 2X to 3X. v15 has a shot at 10X.” Back then, he offered no data, and no third-party study to support his claim. It’s the same thing now.

Tesla says that the new FSD v15—which Musk expects to roll out widely in December—upgrades the neural network that processes the camera sensors into information for the car to drive. It has also swapped the old lo-fi grayscale schematic 3D view for an AI-generated live street scene that looks GTA VI-ish. The latter is the only thing that we know is real—and I have to admit it looks pretty neat—but nobody knows if the new driving engine works as well as Musk claims.

Same song, new version number

It may not matter too much. The new v15 is still Level 2 autonomous driving, which means drivers will need to watch the road at all times. While Musk says it drives better than a human, it must be a very dumb human because Tesla’s own support page says the software “does not make the vehicle autonomous” and is meant for use “only with a fully attentive driver.” That matters because when a person has to be ready to take over the wheel at any second, every avoided crash is just as much a win for the human as for the machine.

Tesla claims that the new FSD offers “25x better handling of safety critical cases.” Better than what? Phil Duan, who leads self-driving at Tesla, said on X that “v15 is 25x safer than v14 across the fleet.” Musk answered an X user, too: “Some people thought we meant 25% improvement; no we mean 25 times!” But we don’t really know about how much “safer” v14 was either. As electric mobility site Electrek points out, without real published figures or a peer-reviewed study—like this one on Waymo reducing its crashes with injured people by 85%—that “25x” claim is hard to substantiate.

In a post, the company explains that its new vision encoder—the part of the network that interprets the information from the car’s video cameras—is the reason for that “25x better handling.” Now shared by FSD, Robotaxis, and Optimus humanoids, the engineering team says the new software improves “the critical intervention rate by 25x.” Tesla says the new encoder was trained on “millions of internet videos.”

According to Tesla, v15 adjusts its speed better in bad weather and school zones, steers clear of deep standing water, and is quicker to spot signs, potholes, small animals, chains, and junk on the road. It doesn’t say anything about fake Looney Tunes-painted tunnels.

It can ease off for speed cameras, too. And it learns from you, so if you cancel the slowdown at the same speed camera twice, by accelerating, it will stop braking at that point of the road. The company also claims that the car’s interior camera—which checks if you are paying attention to the road or not—now works more often when you wear hats and sunglasses.

Neat!

As part of the update, Tesla Reality View has changed. It now looks very similar to the live situational awareness screens you get in some Chinese cars: a hyperrealistic view of the road and your car as seen from behind at a 45-degree angle. You can see vehicles and people in 3D hyperrealistic renderings. Even the buildings are textured and lit like the real thing. It feels like a high-end car racing game. Musk claims “it’s like GTA.”

It looks neat, but it doesn’t seem to convey information better than the older user interface (UI), which showed a much clearer representation of reality. Seen from a high angle, it was a simplified, very stylized version of the road populated with semitransparent versions of vehicles and nearby people. In the old version, despite its perception problems, it was easy to get instant situational awareness. In the new v15, the realism obscures the information with too much darkness and glitz.

The interface also features a blue ribbon that traces the route FSD intends to drive, so you can correct it. Chevron arrows float overhead before every turn. And the map now shows several parking spots at your destination. Some Chinese car manufacturers are already displaying this information directly on the windshield, projecting computer-generated wide-screen augmented-reality (AR) graphics over the real world.

Fortunately, you can switch to a split view or just pick the GPS map view. Musk claims “you can tap any point on the reality revisualizer to make your car go there.” 

Musk says that the new UI uses the same visual features the FSD v15 driving model uses: It’s all AI-generated. The AI model renders short bursts of eight frames at 36 frames per second, using just half of one of the accelerators in the car’s AI4 computer.

Still, the video may lag behind reality because the AI is not fast enough. Musk admits the lag is “a bit high due to compute constraints.” He claims Tesla has a way to trim it by about 35%. More promises.

If December’s wide release arrives on time (which may or may not happen), it will put the new FSD in a lot more hands. In 2027 we will be able to test the real value of Musk’s promises once again. Let’s stay positive. Maybe this will be it. You know what they say: 15th time’s the charm.

#10248. How Nvidia employees feel about Jensen Huang’s return

The public reaction to Jensen Huang’s return has been mixed at best, raising the hackles of lawmakers and corporate governance experts. Even the stock price took a bit of a dip after surging by over 30% on Monday. Within the company, however, the mood appears to be considerably lighter. 

In videos that are circulating across social media, Huang received a hero’s welcome at Nvidia headquarters, where his employees lined the walls cheering for him. Between chants of “Jensen! Jensen!” and “We love you, Jensen,” he addressed his staff in a display of contrition. 

“I’m terribly sorry for putting all of you through all of this,” he said. “I’ve made some very terrible mistakes, and I’m going to work on coming back.” After an employee threw her arms around Huang in a tight hug—lasting over 10 seconds—he continued: “Thank you all for the second chance. I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around.”

Many Nvidia employees have taken to LinkedIn to express their relief over Huang’s return, seemingly overlooking the indiscretions that led to his ousting. They heaped praise on their newly reinstated CEO, describing him as the “heartbeat of Nvidia” and “one of a kind.” 

One employee even invoked Charles Dickens, paraphrasing the opening of A Tale of Two Cities: “It was the worst of times, it is the best of times. It was the season of Darkness, it is the season of Light. It was the winter of despair, it is the spring of hope. We had nothing before us, we have everything before us.”

Another employee claimed he always knew Huang would return to Nvidia: “When Jensen stepped down, many said their goodbyes and thanked him for his legacy. I stayed quiet—not out of indifference, but because deep down I knew there is only one boss, and he would be back.”

A former robotics engineer at Nvidia—who quit rather publicly after Huang’s resignation—congratulated him on X and admitted he made a hasty decision. “Looking back, I may have moved too quickly, and I don’t want to rush into another major decision. For now, I’d like to take some time to rest, reflect, and think carefully about my future. As part of that, I’m open to exploring the possibility of returning.”

These reactions line up with previous reports about employee sentiment after Huang stepped down: According to Wired, many employees showed immediate support for him internally, asking the board to reverse the decision. More than 10,000 current Nvidia employees, or about a quarter of its workforce, signed a petition to reinstate Huang as CEO.

Still, there are some employees who seem to feel differently—perhaps those who have been the target of Huang’s outbursts and creative insults, as reported by The New York Times recently. 

In a Wired report this week, several current and former employees expressed frustration over the turn of events, in part because they had hoped Huang’s exit would usher in some long overdue changes. A number of employees were disturbed by Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy and at least one inappropriate relationship with an employee. 

Beyond that, however, they also felt that Nvidia condoned abusive behavior and echoed previous claims that Huang belittled employees at times. (In an internal post, one employee asserted: “If Jensen comes back, I’m not doing any HR trainings ever again.”) Workers also told Wired that the focus on unity and the “one team” ethos discouraged employees from challenging leadership.

Even employees who have few misgivings about the culture may now find themselves questioning Huang’s leadership. One engineering leader openly grappled with his feelings about Huang in a LinkedIn post he shared before the CEO was reinstated. “Some believe his contributions to Nvidia and the industry are so extraordinary that he deserves another chance,” he wrote. “Others argue that making exceptions for powerful leaders sets a dangerous precedent. I’ve wrestled with this question all week. My opinion has probably changed every single day. And I’ve realized something. I don’t have a clear answer.”

As evidenced by the reception to Huang yesterday, this may not be the prevailing view among employees. But whether or not other employees have lost faith in Huang, there are now open questions about how—if at all—the company plans to address the myriad issues that have been exposed by the events of the last few weeks.

#10245. Americans are sick of disruptive leaders, data shows

Business culture has long lionized bold, disruptive leaders. But these days, at least, Americans are yearning for some stability.   

In a survey conducted shortly after the midterm elections, 82% of Americans said they prefer leaders who “get things back to normal rather than shake things up” and 82% also said they prefer a “stable and predictable” life.

The New York-based global public relations firm Burson interviewed about 1,600 Americans across party lines. The poll was published November 14.

An overwhelming 90% of respondents also said they want honest, calm, consistent leadership, and 75% said they lose respect for CEOs who change positions under pressure.

It is easy to interpret these findings as a reflection of current public opinion about President Donald Trump. Trump’s penchant for disruption and his brash businessman image helped him win the White House twice, but the outcome of the midterms—and the results of the Burson survey—indicate that the public has grown tired of the chaos.

In a separate Associated Press poll, about two-thirds of the roughly 100,000 midterm voters surveyed thought Trump has the wrong priorities, while 7 in 10 said Congress hasn’t been doing enough to check the president’s power.

As Fast Company reported earlier this month, the midterm results also illustrate the risks organizations face when they become overly dependent on a single charismatic leader. Successful leaders can make subordinates increasingly reluctant to question their judgment, even when circumstances change.

“At some point, you have to ask whether people are following your vision, or simply afraid to challenge it,” leadership expert Adam Mendler said.

#10242. Microsoft is shutting down the ‘To Do’ app that replaced Wunderlist, with no real replacement

Microsoft announced this week that its To Do app is shutting down soon, taking the legacy of Wunderlist with it.

Microsoft is shutting down its To Do app at the end of June 2027, with focus moving to the newer Planner app. The company explains:

As we bring personal task management into Planner, we will phase out To Do. The To Do apps will retire on June 30, 2027. Connections that other apps use to access To Do tasks will continue beyond that date, and we’ll provide separate notice before those connections are retired. We’re also updating existing task integrations across Microsoft 365 to connect with Planner, so you’ll be able to create or manage tasks in the Microsoft experiences you already use. Although To Do tasks are already visible in Planner, they will not be migrated to the new private plan. Customers using personal Microsoft accounts will need to choose another app. Our To Do transition guidance  will help you understand what’s changing and plan your next steps.

To Do was built on the foundation of Wunderlist, a wildly popular to do list app that Microsoft purchased in 2015. Wunderlist later shut down in 2020.

Microsoft’s shuffle, notably, leaves general consumers without a replacement app. To Do was available to anyone with a Microsoft account, where Planner is available only to enterprise/business users. So, for long-time Wunderlist users who followed Microsoft migration, this is the end of the road and it’s officially time to move to another app.

#10241. Trump is deploying a special ‘Tiger Team’ for Thanksgiving air travel. Here’s why

Recent chaos is making Americans wary of braving air travel this holiday season, but the Trump administration says it has a plan.

The White House recently announced the formation of a “tiger team” dedicated to preventing major mess-ups like the recent multi-hour ground stop, which snarled airports nationwide as a mountain of delayed and rescheduled flights piled up. The mid-November incident lasted more than four hours, grounding planes all over the country as the federal government scrambled to get the standard lines of communications for air traffic controllers back online. 

Trump’s special interagency group known as the “Transportation Technology Transformation Tiger Team” will bring together representatives from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the Department of Transportation, the Department of Defense, and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, according to the White House. “As millions of Americans prepare to travel for the Thanksgiving holiday, President Donald J. Trump is making sure the skies stay open and the systems run smoothly,” the White House said in a press release.

The FAA reported that 12,462 flights were canceled during the ground stop, which began mid-afternoon on Friday, November 13. The FAA is still investigating the technical hiccup that prompted thousands of planes to be grounded, but a routine router upgrade completed by federal contractor L3Harris Technologies in Arkansas is believed to be at fault.

Tiger teams in action

The term “tiger team” is sometimes used in corporate settings, but it is more commonly used to describe small highly skilled teams convened to solve difficult problems in government and military operations. The most famous tiger team in history is credited with guiding NASA’s Apollo 13 mission back to Earth safely, a feat that earned then-Flight Director (and later NASA Mission Operations Director) Gene Kranz and his specialized group a Presidential Medal of Freedom. 

Other U.S. agencies use tiger teams for specialized problem-solving, including the U.S. Department of Labor. The Trump administration appears to have a particular affinity for the term and also formed a self-described tiger team across the Department of Energy and the Department of the Interior last year to “unleash” the American energy industry. That group later became bogged down wrestling with oil prices and inflation tied to the war in Iran.

Aside from its tongue-twister of a name (try saying it five times fast), very little is known about Trump’s Transportation Technology Transformation Tiger Team. A White House official told The Daily Wire that the FAA is looking into “near-term” network configuration options and other short-term ways to boost the stability of current air traffic control systems while slower modernization efforts move forward. 

“President Trump and Secretary Duffy have brought together the best and the brightest across the government to ensure what happened last Friday can never happen again,” White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said. “This team has hit the ground running in modernizing and improving the reliability of the nation’s decades-old air traffic control system.” 

Schuster claimed that American skies are already safer, thanks to the “tremendous progress” from the tiger team, but reassuring Americans skittish about air safety after a spate of recent scares may not be that easy. Modernizing the U.S. air traffic control system is a major long-term goal pursued by multiple administrations and scores of lawmakers. Yet the ground stop showed that pushing technology fixes into an ancient system that never goes offline carries its own set of risks.

Record holiday travel expected

In a press release, the Transportation Department said it expects to see the “busiest holiday skies in 16 years,” with more than 417,000 flights forecast for the nine days beginning on Monday of Thanksgiving week. Tuesday is projected to be the busiest travel day of the period, with more than 52,000 flights scheduled. 

“From standing up a Tiger Team to ensure a seamless travel experience for fliers to using a successful new platform to predict and address congestion in the airspace, we’ve taken unprecedented action to limit flight delays and cancellations,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said. “The American people can rest assured we will be on the clock 24/7 to get families to their destinations safely and on time.”

#10238. The Jensen Huang saga poses the question: What happens when a leader becomes too big to fail?

Less than a week after Nvidia’s board said it would not reinstate Jensen Huang, it renamed him president and CEO. President Donald Trump had intervened, showing his support for Huang publicly and reportedly even phoning in to a board meeting, urging Nvidia’s directors to reconsider their position.

While Huang is a visionary leader who has delivered extraordinary results, putting him back at the helm despite an open, independent investigation of his conduct may put the company at even greater risk. How will managers hold their teams accountable if the CEO is perceived to be able to violate the company’s code of conduct and lie about it to the board and employees without repercussions?

As an executive and team coach, I’ve seen this situation time and again (albeit not to this extreme), and it creates a near-impossible situation for the rank and file. Leaders must now hold their teams accountable when employees have reason to question that the minimum standards are discretionary.

Why people defend problematic high performers

Compensation was the most submitted question that then-Interim CEO Colette Kress received during last week’s company-wide meeting. And it makes sense—the stock price dropped sharply when Huang announced his resignation.

Yet it’s not just money that likely motivated more than 1,600 comments on an internal post, most supporting Huang’s return. There is also a sense of pride in being part of a winning team, one that was synonymous with Huang. In many ways, defending him may feel like defending what they’ve helped build.

Moreover, with approximately 60 employees reporting directly to Huang, there is no apparent successor—heightening the business risk of replacing him. That, coupled with external political and investor pressure from heavyweights such as Trump, Elon Musk, and Bill Ackman, likely fueled the sentiment that Huang should be reinstated.

What happens when exceptions become precedents

Employees may trust Huang’s business judgment but question how Nvidia handles misconduct. The implications of the board’s reversal will likely take time to fully materialize. For example, what happens when a less indispensable leader violates company policy, or new allegations emerge against Huang or another executive? Will employees become less willing to raise concerns if consequences depend on someone’s perceived value to the company?

Huang’s personal missteps may also erode trust and credibility with employees, after reports that he misled company leaders about his affair with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang have shown he is willing to deceive people in his personal and professional life. Employees may think, What else is he capable of? This may affect employees’ willingness to stake their own reputations behind him.

Managers may also struggle to hold employees to certain expectations when those employees believe exceptions can be made.

One client of mine, whom I’ll call Eliza, is a chief revenue officer who worked with an underperforming VP of sales with a long-standing friendship with the company’s CEO. Although the VP of sales did not perform the basic functions of his role, Eliza couldn’t hold him accountable because the CEO would not back her up. She was responsible for the company’s revenue goal without having the authority to deliver it. Ultimately, Eliza gave the CEO an ultimatum: It was either her or the VP. The CEO ended up moving the VP to another department, but the company nearly lost Eliza in the process. 

Managing a double standard

When Huang returned to the office, an employee shouted, “We love you, Jensen!”

And while his return may be welcome to many, it will create a disparity in expectations that managers will have to address. I once worked with a senior executive in a similar situation. His team’s frustration with the CEO’s decisions became all-consuming—and he agreed with them. He spent his nights and weekends agonizing, and he found himself adding to their list of grievances in team meetings.

He felt awful, and so did his team. I told him he had a decision to make. He could continue with the status quo, or he could acknowledge the reality of the situation and decide whether he wanted to stay or leave the company. 

He ultimately decided to look for a new job, but in the interim he focused his team on what they could influence. While he didn’t disclose to his team that he was looking for work elsewhere, he did tell them that while they worked for this company, they were responsible for having productive conversations that moved the business forward. If anyone felt they couldn’t do that, he would support them if they decided to leave. This alleviated the burden he felt he was carrying by trying to “protect” his team. 

Managers who are in the thankless position of serving under a divisive leader are stuck between a rock and a hard place. They are caught between a leader they can’t remove and their employees. Their best bet is to be clear about where their authority begins and ends, and make it clear that their team, including themselves, will be held to a high standard. But the internal cost of doing this when the company’s leader is not held to the same standard is high; it creates a ripe breeding ground for talented managers and employees to leave.

While it is rare for a company to be ensnared in a scandal of this magnitude, leaders often face pressure to overlook the behavior of someone who delivers exceptional results. Overlooking this behavior may seem like the easiest path for continuing to deliver exceptional results—but it comes with a cost: the well-being of the rest of the team. This is why adequate succession planning is so critical, so no one becomes “too big to fail.”

#10236. Build Live Video Chat With WebRTC: From First Call to Production Debugging

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Adding real-time video to a web app used to mean plugins, proprietary SDKs and a lot of money. Today every modern browser ships with WebRTC, a set of APIs that lets two browsers exchange audio, video and data directly. The catch is that WebRTC gives you building blocks, not a finished feature. This guide walks through those blocks in the order you actually need them, with the exact API calls you need, and then covers the production issues that tutorials usually skip.

A browser-to-browser call has four moving parts:

Start with the local preview. Browsers only allow camera access on HTTPS or localhost, so serve your page accordingly.

1.     Request a stream with navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia(), passing video constraints (an ideal width of 1280 and height of 720 is a sensible default) and audio constraints with echoCancellation and noiseSuppression enabled.

2.     Assign the returned MediaStream to the srcObject property of your local video element.

3.     Keep a reference to the stream, because you will add its tracks to the peer connection later.

Set the muted and playsinline attributes on the local video element. Without muted users hear themselves, and without playsinline iOS Safari opens the video full screen.

The peers need a way to find each other. A tiny Node.js server using the ws package is enough for development. Its whole job is to relay messages between the peers in a room:

1.     Create a WebSocket server (for example with the ws package) listening on its own port.

2.     Keep a map of room names to the set of sockets in each room.

3.     When a client sends a join message, store the room name on the socket and add it to that room's set.

4.     For every other message type, forward the raw message to the other sockets in the same room, and never echo it back to the sender.

5.     On disconnect, remove the socket from its room so stale peers do not receive messages.

In production you would add authentication, limit room size to two for one-to-one calls, and validate message types, but the shape stays the same.

Both sides create an RTCPeerConnection, add their local tracks and listen for the remote ones:

1.     Create a new RTCPeerConnection with an iceServers list that contains at least one STUN server.

2.     Loop over the local stream's tracks and call addTrack() for each one.

3.     In the ontrack handler, attach the first remote stream to your remote video element.

4.     In the onicecandidate handler, send every new candidate to the other peer through your signalling channel as a candidate message.

One peer creates an offer, the other answers, and both apply each other's descriptions. Candidates arrive asynchronously in the background.

1.     The caller runs createOffer(), applies it with setLocalDescription() and sends the description as an offer message.

2.     The callee applies the offer with setRemoteDescription(), runs createAnswer(), applies it locally and sends it back as an answer.

3.     The caller applies the answer with setRemoteDescription().

4.     Both sides pass every incoming candidate message to addIceCandidate().

If both peers might start a call at the same time, look up the "perfect negotiation" pattern on MDN. It assigns one side as polite and resolves offer collisions cleanly instead of leaving both peers stuck.

On a home network, STUN alone often works. On corporate Wi-Fi, mobile carriers and symmetric NATs it frequently does not, and the call silently fails to connect. A TURN server relays media when a direct path is impossible. The open-source coturn server is the usual choice.

In practice, your iceServers list should contain your own STUN URL plus a TURN URL with a username and credential, so the browser can fall back to the relay automatically when direct connectivity fails.

Generate short-lived TURN credentials on your backend rather than hard-coding them, and budget for bandwidth: relayed calls pass every frame through your server.

Users deny camera access, unplug headsets and switch from Wi-Fi to 4G mid-call. Catch NotAllowedError and show a clear explanation, listen for devicechange events, and use RTCRtpSender.replaceTrack() to swap cameras without renegotiating the whole call.

Listen to pc.onconnectionstatechange. When the state becomes disconnected, wait a few seconds before giving up, because it often recovers. On failed, call pc.restartIce() to try new network paths.

Use RTCRtpSender.setParameters() to cap the bitrate on weak connections, and read pc.getStats() to monitor packet loss and round-trip time. Showing a small "poor connection" indicator does more for perceived quality than any codec tweak.

Mesh calls, where every participant connects to every other, work for two or three people. Beyond that, upload bandwidth explodes. Group calls need a Selective Forwarding Unit (SFU) such as mediasoup, LiveKit or Janus, which receives each stream once and forwards it to the others.

Tutorials end at a working demo, but the fastest way to understand what production WebRTC looks like is to watch a real call from the inside. Chrome ships an internal diagnostics page that shows every peer connection the browser opens, and it works on any site that uses WebRTC.

1.     Open chrome://webrtc-internals in one tab and keep it open.

2.     In another tab, start a call on your own demo and find its RTCPeerConnection entry.

3.     Expand that entry and look at the ICE candidate pairs: you will see whether the call went direct (host or srflx) or through a TURN relay (relay).

4.     Open the stats graphs for the outbound video stream and watch the bitrate, frame rate and resolution adapt when you throttle the network in DevTools.

5.     Check the negotiated codec and how quickly the connection recovers when you switch Wi-Fi off and back on.

Once you can read your own call, repeat the exercise on a production service. Any browser-based product works, whether a meeting tool or a live video chat that pairs two visitors, because webrtc-internals shows the same data for every site. Expect differences from your demo: more candidate pairs, a relay candidate in the list and a bitrate that adapts faster. Seeing them makes the earlier sections concrete, from why TURN matters to how bandwidth estimation reacts to packet loss.

The one-to-one call above is the core of many products, from telehealth consultations and tutoring to customer support. The engineering challenges grow with the use case: random matching needs queueing and presence on the signalling server, public platforms need moderation and reporting, and global audiences need TURN servers in several regions.

Start with the minimal version, get it working across Chrome, Firefox and Safari on both desktop and mobile, and add TURN before real users arrive. Once the call is reliable, every other feature becomes a much easier problem.

#10234. Expect Samsung’s good-value Galaxy devices to get more expensive, report says

Rising memory costs are hitting mid-range devices the hardest. The latest report suggests Samsung will increase the price of its Galaxy A device series by 19% next year.

The report comes from Korean news outlet SEDaily. An industry source has reportedly stated that Samsung plans to increase the price of its mid-range phones starting next year. More specifically, the Galaxy A series.

The range between price jumps varies across a reported 8 Galaxy A series devices, but the highest value difference nearly hits a notable 19% increase. The largest jump reaches 18.6% for the Galaxy A17, which could increase from $269 to $319. It would no longer sit in a sub-$300 spot and wouldn’t be much of a value buy anymore.

Again, these are phones praised for sitting at a convenient price point. Samsung’s Galaxy A devices are generally good value and offer a lot of the best One UI features for a price that doesn’t come close to the current flagship selling points.

This comes after a report came out last month indicating Samsung cut production of its Galaxy A devices by “approximately 20%.” Memory makes up more of the overall component cost in mid-range devices. So the cost of the overall device is more influenced by memory prices than in a flagship, like the Galaxy S26 Ultra. Even with a specced-out build, there’s more dispersion of costly components, rather than one expensive component like memory taking up the bulk of the production price.

That cut is estimated to be around 10 million units, and this latest report only furthers the claim that mid-range devices are too costly to make for Samsung.

The opposite is true for the Galaxy S27 Pro and Ultra, which reportedly got the green light for increased production prior to launch. Price suggestions average an increase of $200 for the Galaxy S27 and Galaxy S27 Plus. As for the high-spec Galaxy S27 Pro and Ultra, they start at $1,399 and $1,499, respectively.

There was already a massive disparity between those devices and the increasingly validated Galaxy A devices, and the gap is shrinking.

#10233. Billy Evans may have gotten a share of the profits from ‘You Can See Everything’ after all

You Can See Everything may begin as a documentary about disgraced tech entrepreneur Elizabeth Holmes in the month before her prison sentence, but in the movie’s second half, an entirely different (and entirely meta) subject emerges: the deal between Holmes’s partner, Billy Evans, and studio A24 to give Evans a cut of the film’s profits, and codirector Nathan Fielder’s uncertainty about how much Holmes knows about the money.

Given Evans’s status as the film’s quasi-villain, the thought that ticket buyers’ money would end up in his pockets had moviegoers squirming in their seats. Thankfully, the documentary ends with a title card saying that Evans “decided to give up his right to profit on the movie” shortly after filming concluded. 

But a new investigation says that Evans didn’t fully forgo his payout from the film—it was just redirected to charity instead.

Evans’s share of the profits

Two anonymous sources told The Hollywood Reporter that Evans and A24 amended their agreement so his payout would go to an unnamed children’s charity, not directly into his bank account. An A24 representative later confirmed that this deal was made, though they didn’t say why that detail was omitted from the film’s final title card.

The exact size of Evans’s payout remains unknown, but given You Can See Everything’s unprecedented success at the box office, his share is definitely more than small change. This week, the film crossed $100 million in global box-office revenue, making it the fifth-highest-grossing non-concert documentary of all time.

In a separate interview for THR, Evans explained why he agreed to back out on his initial deal with A24.

“They said that it would help the project. Time and time again, when there’s things that I really didn’t want to do that they said would be helpful for making a better movie and helping people see Liz more clearly, I made those sacrifices or decisions to help the project,” Evans said. “I am totally stubborn, but if there’s anything that I can do to help Liz regardless of the cost, I will do it.”

Why the directors disagree

Though THR’s report frames You Can See Everything’s final title card as disingenuous, directors Fielder and Lance Oppenheim say the outlet’s story misses the mark.

At a Q&A on November 21, Fielder and Oppenheim reportedly said the story’s wording was inaccurate and that none of the documentary’s subjects were paid, according to reporting by Semafor.

A studio source later told Semafor that Evans fully relinquished his profit-sharing deal, and that the charitable donation was a separate, mutual agreement between Evans and A24.

Meanwhile, THR’s editor-in-chief, Maer Roshan, defended the story over email, saying that A24’s perspective “seems like a pretty semantic argument.”

Despite the fact that Moto Tag 2 has only been on the market for a few months at this point, Motorola is apparently getting Moto Tag 3 out in the not-too-distant future, and it’s already on sale (probably by mistake).

An Amazon UK listing went up this week for “Moto Tag 3,” a new version of Motorola’s Android Find Hub tracker. The listing shows the tracker in “Pantone Lucent White,” while a second image shared by Evan Blass shows the new model in a vibrant purple color.

There’s no indication of major changes in “Moto Tag 3,” with Motorola still claiming similar battery life, using a CR2032 battery, and supporting UWB in Android Find Hub.

“Moto Tag 3” is on sale from Amazon UK, though it comes with a “1-4 month” shipping estimate. This is almost certainly a slip-up, especially given the timing.

This comes much earlier than expected. The original Moto Tag launched in 2024, with its sequel being announced in early 2026 before going on sale in the US less than six months ago in June 2026. Such an early move to “Moto Tag 3” is interesting, to say the least, so we’ll have to wait and see if there are any changes in tow beyond just the new colors. That said, these are really nice colors. It’s also possible this is just the same model with a slip-up in branding – the model number on the Amazon listing is unchanged.

We’ll have to wait and see what happens. Moto Tag 2 did debut at CES in January, and with Razr Flex also in the works, Motorola almost certainly would launch an updated tracker at the trade show if it truly does plan to do so soon.
